newsitem.title: USA: Fed Governor says 2.5 pct growth rate safest.
newsitem.headline: Fed Governor says 2.5 pct growth rate safest.

text.p: Outgoing Federal Reserve Board Governor Lawrence Lindsey said on Saturday that the U.S. economy should not grow faster than 2.5 percent, or it could risk pushing inflation beyond a workable rate of 3 percent.

Appearing on CNN's "Evans and Novak" show, Lindsey said, "I'm trying to maintain a rate of growth that allows for real growth of about 2.5 percent, and inflation that's something under 3 ... I think given the current environment, that is as fast as we could probably safely grow."
Although Lindsey denied in the interview that economic growth was being targeted to prevent a too-robust environment, he said he was targeting nominal GDP.

The U.S. economy slowed last year to a growth rate of 2.1 percent in the third quarter. The last quarter of 1996 is expected to show a continued moderate growth rate. The first official estimate for fourth-quarter economic growth will be made later this month.

Lindsey, whose unexpected resignation from the board was announced on Friday, also said that a balanced budget was not the key to a sound economy. He said that improving the quality of what the government spends money on was more important than a balanced budget.

"I don't think that the balanced budget is the key. I think what's much more important is what we spend the money on," said Lindsey. "If government were to spend money on things that were actually productive yielding a high rate of return, I'd be all for taking money from the private sector and moving it to the public sector."
Republican Lindsey is leaving the central bank after five years to join the conservative American Enterprise Institute.
Lindsey said he was leaving the board "with every confidence that the economy and the Fed is in good hands."
Lindsey noted that the U.S. economy was entering its seventh year of expansion, and that so far, there had been no major mistakes on either the monetary or fiscal fronts.

The Fed Governor said that while the current consumer debt load and record rate of consumer bankruptcies were a concern, he said that the central bank had been on top of the problem for two years now, and he thought any major negative economic impacts from consumer debt could be avoided.
"With any luck, we have ducked any major macroeconomic effects from the consumer debt problem," Lindsey said.

Lindsey, who has long been an advocate of low taxes, said too much non-productive activity was being spent on trying to avoid taxes, and that the current capital gains tax structure had an adverse effect on the economy.
Lindsey said that significantly lowering the capital gains tax would "probably boost the long term growth rate by a few tenths of a point."

A lowering of the government's Consumer Price Index would also help the economy, Lindsey said. He agreed with recent studies that contend the CPI overstates inflation, but he noted that it would be a political decision for the administration to accept a lower CPI rate and reduce payments tied to the CPI.

Lindsey did not express concern about recent activity of the financial markets, saying that "markets always move towards the equilibrium." He said the key for the U.S. economy was not what Wall Street did in the short term, but the long term policies of the nation.
"Markets go up and down, as we learned in this country in '87. You can have big changes and the economy will move forward. What really matters is the long-term and not the short-term," he said.
